summary:
Keegan McCallum (founder of uRun) opens by reframing the generative video conversation away from the quality axis exemplified by the Will Smith spaghetti clip, Sora, Sora 2, and SeeDance, and toward efficiency and long-horizon capability. He demos Helios, uRun's distillation of Wan 2.1 14B, rendering a continuous real-time stream in one window while discrete pre-generated clips play in another, noting the slower clip has better motion despite costing roughly a hundred times more to produce. He places Helios within a 2025 explosion of at least forty models offering real-time or long-horizon generation, spanning world models, avatar models (lemon slice), and real-time video-to-video transformation.

He anchors pricing: $10 buys roughly three hours of continuous generation; $50 buys about fifteen hours. Compared with a show of hands revealing attendees who burn $10–$50 of coding tokens in an hour, he argues this cost profile unlocks new interaction patterns: magic mirrors (e.g., previewing haircuts or outfits via webcam), accessible visual mediums for non-text thinkers, and content creation that replaces slot-machine prompting with sub-second live steering, optionally upscaled via models like Google Gemini Omni.

Building such applications requires global GPU placement, WebRTC with ICE and TURN, and multiple models wired into continuously streaming pipelines synchronized to user controls. uRun's pitch is a drop-in React component, a programmable Python runtime for async pipelines, and a CLI/MCP server so agents can compose these interactive video applications. McCallum notes he finished well under time and recruits design partners and hires.

sections.title: Generative video along the quality axis
sections.summary: Keegan introduces uRun as an inference provider focused on interactive media. He recaps the quality-axis progress from the Will Smith spaghetti clip (2023) to Sora, Sora 2, and SeeDance, motivating a pivot to another improvement axis.

sections.title: The other axis: efficiency and long horizons
sections.summary: He demos Helios, uRun's distill of Wan 2.1 14B, rendering continuous real-time video alongside pre-generated clips at last year's frontier quality. The slower clip arguably has better motion but costs roughly 100× more. He situates Helios (released March) among 40+ 2025 models with real-time or long-horizon capability, including world models, avatar models (lemon slice), and video-to-video transformation models.

sections.title: What ten dollars of generation buys now
sections.summary: After a show of hands showing many attendees burn $10–$50 of coding tokens in an hour, he anchors new pricing: $10 for ~3 hours and $50 for ~15 hours of continuous generated video, framing this as a full day interacting with a visual-medium AI.

sections.title: Magic mirrors, accessibility, and steering shots live
sections.summary: He outlines interaction shapes unlocked by cheap real-time video: magic mirrors (webcam try-on of outfits, cars, haircuts), accessible visual mediums for non-text thinkers, and content creation that replaces slot-machine prompting with sub-second steering, optionally upscaled via Gemini Omni. He gestures at world models as a broader horizon.

sections.title: The hard part is serving it
sections.summary: He details serving requirements: GPUs positioned globally, WebRTC with ICE and TURN, and multiple models wired into continuous streaming pipelines synchronized frame-by-frame with user controls. uRun offers a drop-in React component, a programmable async Python runtime, and a CLI/MCP server so agents can build these applications. He closes under time, recruiting design partners and hires.

demonstrations: Side-by-side demo of Helios continuous real-time generation versus a batch of pre-generated clips at last year's frontier quality.

limitations: Demo comparisons mix real-time streams with pre-generated clips, not direct quality head-to-heads.

Global low-latency serving remains hard; requires distributed GPUs and WebRTC/ICE/TURN infrastructure.
